A hotter-than-expected September inflation report has put a dampener on the mood in markets today.

Earlier today, the consumer price index rose 3.7% in September from an annual rate of 3.4% in August. Economists polled by the Wall Street Journal had expected a 3.6% increase. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, also topped economists' forecasts.

The data raises pressure on the Federal Reserve to consider further interest-rate increases to tame inflation, which is sitting well above its 2% target.

Investors are also dissecting a fresh round of earnings from Wall Street. Bank of America shares are tumbling after its profit disappointed even excluding a $1.2 billion fine, while Morgan Stanley's and BlackRock's shares are also lower despite stronger quarterly results.

CoreWeave, one of the riskier stocks in the AI basket, was taking a dive today after a chart of its bond yields went viral on X, sparking concerns about its long-term ability to remain solvent.

As of 1:00 p.m., the stock was down 14.4% on the news, dragging down peers like Nebius, Oracle, and IREN with it.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Rising rates are testing CoreWeave

CoreWeave's business model relies on borrowing money to spend on chips and data centers to then rent out that computing capacity. The company already has $35 billion in debt, and its interest expense is driving steep losses.

Investor Chamath Palihapitiya posted a chart on X yesterday, showing that CoreWeave's bond yield had reached a new all-time high at 15%, up from 9% this summer, as bond yields in general have risen. Palihapitiya suggested a private credit bubble could be forming, and Elon Musk replied "Yikes" to the post.

The 15% rate is just one loan, but the post did spark some alarm about neocloud stocks generally, as they're likely to face pressure if rates continue to go up.

What's next for CoreWeave

After Nvidia had to step into support its IPO, CoreWeave soared in its first months on the market, but the stock is now trading near a 52-week low even as the broader AI sector has continued to rise.

If interest rates continue to move higher, it will be even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit, and its debt could eventually unravel. Thus far, the company has continued to post strong top-line growth, and it's expected to deliver 159% revenue growth to $3.54 billion in its third-quarter earnings report.

That shows CoreWeave doesn't have a demand problem, but the concerns about its debt are rational. Expect the pressure on the stock to continue unless rates ease or the company makes progress on the bottom line.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock tumbled an unlucky 7% through 10:10 a.m. ET this morning -- and here's the weird thing: It did this right after Mizuho analyst Siti Panigrahi reiterated his "outperform" rating on the stock and confirmed he still thinks Oracle shares are worth $320.

But the stock only costs $133 today!

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Oracle.

Mizuho still loves Oracle stock

That's a strange reaction to a buy rating, I must say. So how do we explain it?

According to Panigrahi, Oracle is making "continued construction progress" on its Project Jupiter -- the gigantic AI data center it's building in the New Mexico desert for $165 billion. It has proposed rerouting the gas pipeline that supplies power to the data center (via Bloom Energy fuel cells) to avoid restarting its environmental review.

The analyst is optimistic this effort will succeed, but notes that investors will need to wait for further updates on Oct. 28.

What's next for Oracle

Problem is... investors don't seem interested in waiting. They're selling first and asking questions later.

Why? As StreetInsider.com reminds us today, Oracle recently suffered a credit rating downgrade to BBB- (one notch above "speculative") on worries that the company is spending too much on capital investment to build Project Jupiter, with little revenue to offset its costs. OpenAI isn't required to make payments for the data center before 2027, and Oracle's cash situation could look tenuous in the meantime.

S&P Global Market Intelligence data show Oracle with $37.1 billion in cash currently, burning nearly $29 billion a year, and at risk of needing to add to its $169.1 billion debt load. Mizuho may be right that the stock will be undervalued. The question is whether Oracle can survive long enough for investors to realize that value?

title: Will Rising Capex Weigh on Oracle's Free Cash Flow Outlook?
detail:
Will Rising Capex Weigh on Oracle's Free Cash Flow Outlook?
Vasundhara Sawalka
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 8:02 AM CDT 3 min read
ORCL
AMZN
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Oracle's ORCL aggressive AI infrastructure buildout has put its free cash flow (FCF) outlook under scrutiny. In first-quarter fiscal 2027, capital expenditures jumped to $28.5 billion from $8.5 billion a year ago, pushing FCF to negative $5.4 billion despite record operating cash flow of $23 billion, up 184% year over year. Net of customer prepayments, cash capex was about $18 billion.

Guidance indicates the pressure will persist. Oracle reiterated fiscal 2027 capex of $90-$95 billion, with net cash capex capped at $70 billion, and has not set a timeline for FCF to turn positive after a negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026. The company plans to raise about $40 billion in debt and equity this year, including a $20 billion at-the-market stock sale completed in the first quarter, which dilutes shareholders. Gross margin is also expected to decline in fiscal 2027 as new sites ramp.

Still, the demand backdrop supports the spending. Remaining performance obligations rose $209 billion year over year to $664 billion, aided by more than $30 billion in new AI cloud contracts that Oracle said require no incremental capital raising and largely affect capex only from fiscal 2028. The company delivered 850 megawatts of capacity and more than 300,000 GPUs, while cloud infrastructure revenues surged 121% to $7.4 billion. Management expects projects to generate strong FCF soon after ramping, with conversion potentially near 100% of post-tax EBITDA.

For second-quarter fiscal 2027, Oracle expects total revenue growth of 30-34% and cloud revenue growth of 65-71% in USD, with non-GAAP EPS of $1.85-$1.93. Full-year revenues are now projected at a minimum of $90 billion, with non-GAAP EPS raised to $8.10 from $8.05. While the revenue trajectory is encouraging, FCF is likely to remain negative in the near term, making capex discipline and the upcoming Oct. 28 Investor Day key to watch.

How ORCL's Capex Strategy Compares With Microsoft & Amazon

Oracle's cash-flow strain mirrors a broader AI spending wave among U.S. hyperscalers. Microsoft MSFT spent $41 billion on capex, including finance leases, in fourth-quarter fiscal 2026, up 69% year over year, yet Microsoft still generated $19.6 billion in FCF, though down 23%. Microsoft expects FCF to stay positive in fiscal 2027. Amazon AMZN raised its 2026 capex outlook to $220 billion from $200 billion after second-quarter capex climbed to $54.2 billion from $32.1 billion. Consequently, Amazon's trailing 12-month FCF swung to an outflow of $7.6 billion from an inflow of $18.2 billion, leaving Amazon's cash profile closer to Oracle's current position.

Oracle (ORCL) is one of the stocks most watched by Zacks.com visitors lately. So, it might be a good idea to review some of the factors that might affect the near-term performance of the stock.

Shares of this software maker have returned +2% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +2.1% change. The Zacks Computer - Software industry, to which Oracle belongs, has gained 7.9% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Revisions to Earnings Estimates

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

Oracle is expected to post earnings of $1.88 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of -16.8%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed +0%.

The consensus earnings estimate of $8.13 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +6.6%. This estimate has changed +1.8% over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $10.87 indicates a change of +33.8% from what Oracle is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for Oracle.
